texts.facts: Challenging the Regulation 2.3.12 of the Food Safety and Standards (Prohibition and Restriction on Sale) Regulations, 2011 dated 25.06.2019, which prohibits sale of the common salt for direct human consumption as well as Regulation 2.4.42 of the Food Safety Standards (Packaging and Labelling) Regulations, 2011, this writ petition is filed seeking to declare those Regulations as null and void and ultra vires of the Constitution of India with a consequential direction to the respondents 1 to 3 to permit the petitioner to have the following label bearing words 'Non-Iodised Common Salt' on the package of Common Salt and on the package of Iodised Salt as 'Iodised salt-A Necessary Nutrient'. 2. The facts leading to the filing of the writ petition are as follows: 2.1. Originally, the petitioner-salt association filed this writ petition to quash the Regulation 2.3.12 dated 31.07.2018 banning the common salt for human consumption as null and void. Later, by an amendment dated 25.06.2019, the prohibition was mandated for direct human consumption and consumption related activities. The respondents' counter affidavits dealt with labelling procedures also. Therefore, the petitioner has amended the prayer. 2.2. According to the petitioner, this is the third round of wrongful amendment arbitrarily done by the respondents. In the first round of litigation, when the ban on sale of common salt was introduced through Rule 44-I of PFA Rules in the year 2005, the challenge to it went upto the Supreme Court. The fact remains that the Tuticorin Salt Association, being the second biggest association in the Country next to Gujarat, was neither consulted nor called for revisiting the matter with technical and scientific data and so on. In the Thuthukudi Thanpadu Uppu Ettrumathi ... vs Union Of India on 13 August, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/151339691/ 3 meantime, the impugned amendment came to be passed. As per the Indian Council of Medical Research (2010) publication namely, 'Nutrient requirement and Recommended dietary allowances for Indians', the Recommended Daily Allowances of (RDA) of iodine for different physiological age groups including Pregnant & Lactating Women ranges from 90g/d to 250g/d. The Iodine content of commonly used plant food is very low and far below the Recommended Dietary Allowances (RDA). Further, the amount of thiocyanate, a goitrogen, is high in plant foods which affect the iodine utilization in the human system. Therefore, iodine supplementation to the entire population is essential. Surveys conducted by several agencies including Directorate General of Health Services, ICMR, State Govts. & Health Institutions have revealed that no State/UT in India is free from Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDD). Out of 427 districts surveyed (up to 2017-18) in all the https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 19/08/2025 03:06:03 pm ) 29 States and 7 Union Territories so far, 348 districts are endemic i.e where the prevalence of Iodine Deficiency Disorders (IDDs) is more than 5%. Due to soil erosion, there is a deficiency of iodine in foods including cereals, pulses, fruits, vegetables etc grown on such soil. The famous Kangra valley study conducted by AllMS, New Delhi, from 1956 to 1972 proved beyond doubt that lodised salt given to defined population of the district brought down prevalence of Goitre from 40% to 5% within a few years. The success of this study lead to launch of National Goitre Control Programme (NGCP) in 1962 by the Government of India. Consumption of iodated salt is the cheapest method to control Iodine Deficiency Disorders in the country. Salt is best medium for supply of iodine to the entire population since it is universally consumed by all the population. WHO and UNICEF have also recommended universal salt iodization since 1993, as stated in WHO guidelines.
